The Battle of Hattin. On the fourth of July, eleven eighty-seven, Saladin's Muslim forces decisively defeated the combined armies of the Kingdom of Jerusalem in the Levant. Near the village of Hattin west of the Sea of Galilee, Saladin commanded roughly twelve thousand troops against a Crusader army of about twenty thousand led by King Guy of Lusignan.

Saladin was a master of strategy. He lured Guy of Lusignan into a catastrophic trap by cutting off his army's retreat to water in the Horns of Hattin, a desolate and rocky terrain. In the crushing heat, the Crusaders became desperate. They were dehydrated and exhausted when Saladin's final assault broke them utterly. Many of the captured knights and nobles were executed after surrendering. The catastrophic losses forced the Crusaders to abandon their strongest fortifications, including the city of Jerusalem itself, which fell to Saladin shortly after.

The defeat was so severe that it prompted the Third Crusade, a massive effort led by Richard the Lionheart from eleven eighty-nine to eleven ninety-two, yet even this could not recover Jerusalem permanently for Christian hands. Hattin demonstrated Saladin's superior strategy and his deep understanding of logistics and psychology. He was one of history's greatest military commanders, and his victory at Hattin turned the entire tide of the Crusades. The Holy Land would never again be fully under Christian control, and the shadow of Hattin would haunt the Crusader project for centuries to come.
